unit.title: Support continuous improvement systems and processes

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: An electrical contractor in Montego Bay says it has a 'continuous improvement system'. What does this mean in practice?
options: A one-off review done only when a big client complains
A rule that every job must be done faster each month
A plan to buy brand new tools every single year, whatever their state
A regular way of finding, testing and keeping better methods

questions.stem: Why do small, steady improvements often work better on site than one big change?
options: They never need any money or any time at all
They are easier to try, check and keep going
They let managers skip talking with the crew
They mean that the results need not be measured

questions.stem: A crew tries out a new way of labelling circuits on two jobs to see if it works. In the PDCA cycle, which step is this trial?
options: Do
Plan
Check
Act

questions.stem: The trial worked, so the new labelling method is written into the company procedure for every crew. Which PDCA step is this?
options: Plan
Check
Act
Do

questions.stem: Before changing the way final test results are recorded, why measure how often errors happen now?
options: So you can show later whether the change helped
So the crew knows exactly who made the most errors last month
So the old method can be kept no matter what
So the test instruments can be recalibrated

questions.stem: Which is the simplest tool for a crew to tally how often each type of defect is found during inspections?
options: A pie chart of the company's yearly costs
A Gantt chart of next month's jobs
The supplier's price list
A check sheet with a tally for each defect

questions.stem: A Pareto chart of callback causes shows that loose terminations and wrong breaker sizes cause most callbacks. What should the team do?
options: Work on every cause equally, all at the same time
Start with the causes that happen the least often
Work first on the few causes giving most callbacks
Stop recording callbacks, as the chart is now done

questions.stem: A client's RCD keeps tripping. Why does the team ask 'why?' several times (the 5 whys) when looking into it?
options: To find someone on the crew to blame for it
To get past the symptom to the real cause
To make the meeting last for a set time
To avoid having to test the installation

questions.stem: In a fishbone (cause and effect) diagram about jobs finishing late, what is written at the 'head' of the fish?
options: The name of the crew leader
The problem: jobs finished late
The cost of all the materials
The date of the next meeting

questions.stem: An electrician walks back to the van six times during one job to fetch parts. Which kind of waste is this?
options: Motion: unnecessary movement
Overproduction: making too much
Defects: work that must be redone
Inventory: too much stock held

questions.stem: Which of these is waste caused by defects in electrical work?
options: Planning the cable route before starting
Testing each circuit before handover
Labelling every way of the distribution board
Going back to re-terminate a loose neutral

questions.stem: Long off-cuts of cable are thrown away on every job. Which improvement would most reduce this waste?
options: Buy the cheapest cable that can be found in the shops
Order twice as much cable as is needed
Measure runs from the drawings and plan cuts
Stop using cable drums on site altogether

questions.stem: A crew sorts out its van, removes broken and unused items, and gives every tool a marked place. What is this method called?
options: Just-in-time delivery
Benchmarking
5S workplace organisation
Value engineering

questions.stem: In 5S, why is the last step, 'sustain', often the hardest?
options: People slip back to old habits unless checks go on
It needs the most expensive equipment of all five steps
It can only ever be done by the manager
It must be done once and then never again

questions.stem: Why should the electricians who do the work be involved in improving the method?
options: So the manager will have less work to do
They know the real problems and will own the change
So that nobody can blame the manager later on
Because the law says every worker must vote on it

questions.stem: A crew member, Tanisha, suggests colour-coded cable ties for each type of circuit. What is the best first response?
options: Tell her it is not her job to suggest any changes
Adopt it on every site at once, without testing it
Say it is a good idea but then do nothing more
Thank her, and agree a small trial to test it

questions.stem: Why should the results of an improvement be fed back to the person who suggested it?
options: It shows ideas are valued, so more are offered
So that the person can be paid an extra bonus each month
So the idea can be stopped without a reason
Because feedback is only given for poor ideas

questions.stem: A new method for recording test results has been approved. What is the best way to roll it out?
options: Email the form and expect everyone to work it out alone
Leave the old and new forms in use side by side
Brief the crews, show the method, update the procedure
Tell only the newest staff, since they learn faster

questions.stem: Why should crews be told the reason for a change, not only the new steps?
options: So that they can choose not to follow it
So the briefing takes a little longer
So the old method can be kept as well
People follow a change better if they see why

questions.stem: Three months after a new handover checklist was brought in, callbacks have not fallen. What should happen next?
options: Declare the checklist a success all the same
Check it is used, and look for other causes
Scrap every checklist used in the company
Stop measuring callbacks from now on

questions.stem: Callbacks fell from 12 a quarter to 9 a quarter after a change. By what percentage did they fall?
Before a change, roughing-in a house took 40 hours on average. Now it takes 34 hours. What is the saving per house?
options: 4 hours
34 hours
74 hours
6 hours

questions.stem: Which chart best shows whether a measure, such as weekly callbacks, is improving over time?
options: A run chart (line graph) over the weeks
A single pie chart showing the results for one week only
A photo of the crew at work on site
A list of the names of the crew

questions.stem: A better method for installing ceiling fans has been proved in a trial. How is it made the normal way of working?
options: By telling one of the crews about it at lunch on a Friday afternoon
By keeping it in the crew leader's head
By writing it into the procedure and training all crews
By letting each crew decide whether to use it

questions.stem: A procedure was improved last month, but an old printed copy is still kept in one van. What is the risk?
options: None, as both copies say almost the same thing
The van will be harder to keep tidy and clean
The crew will finish its jobs far too quickly
The crew may follow the old, poorer method

questions.stem: How can client feedback help a contractor improve?
options: It shows problems the crew may not see itself
It replaces the need for any inspection of the work by the crew
It decides each worker's pay rise
It is only useful when it is all good

questions.stem: In continuous improvement, what is benchmarking?
options: Fixing a work bench firmly to the workshop floor
Marking a level line on a wall before fixing boxes
Comparing your results with the best to find gaps
Setting the right height for a test bench

questions.stem: A near miss is reported: a worker nearly touched a live terminal on a board that was wrongly labelled. How should this be used for improvement?
options: Ignore it, because nobody was hurt
Find the cause, fix labelling and share the lesson
Punish the worker who reported it
Keep it quiet so that the client does not hear about it at all

questions.stem: A proposed time-saving change would mean checking the voltage tester on a proving unit only once a day. What should you do?
options: Reject it, as it removes a key safety step
Trial it on a few jobs to see what happens
Accept it, since time is money
Let each electrician decide for himself

questions.stem: Which is the best source of ideas for improving the company's work?
options: Only the managing director's own ideas
Only ideas from other contractors' adverts
Only ideas that cost nothing at all
Staff, clients, data, audits and incidents

questions.stem: Two improvement ideas are put forward, but there is time for only one this quarter. How should the team choose?
options: Pick the idea put forward by the most senior person
Pick the idea that sounds the most modern
Compare the benefit, cost, effort and risk
Toss a coin so that the choice is fair

questions.stem: A cable label printer costs J$180,000 and saves J$15,000 a month in rework. How many months until it pays for itself?
options: 6 months
12 months
15 months
18 months

questions.stem: Why keep a written record of each improvement project, including what did not work?
options: So the records can be thrown away later
So the team can blame someone if it fails
So nobody else ever needs to be trained
So others can learn and not repeat mistakes

questions.stem: An experienced electrician who knows the history of a hotel's installation is about to retire. What should the team do?
options: Capture what he knows in notes and drawings
Nothing, as the next person will learn in time
Ask him to keep it secret from the new staff
Throw out the old drawings that he used

questions.stem: Where is the best place to keep the crews' lessons learned, so that every crew can use them?
options: On each worker's own mobile phone
On scraps of paper kept in the vans
In a shared, organised file or database
In the memory of the crew leader

questions.stem: Some senior electricians resist a new testing form, saying 'the old way works'. What is the best approach?
options: Force it on them with warnings of discipline
Hear their concerns and show the benefits
Let them keep the old form for ever
Leave them out of the meetings about it

questions.stem: Which helps most to keep a crew motivated during an improvement project?
options: Hiding all the results until the end
Changing the targets every single week
Giving all the credit to the manager
Sharing progress and recognising effort

questions.stem: As a lead electrician, what is your main part in the company's continuous improvement system?
options: Put agreed changes into practice and report results
Write the company's mission statement and its vision for the future
Decide the company's prices and its profits
Approve the company's yearly accounts

questions.stem: An audit finds that 1 in every 10 test certificates has a missing reading. What is the best improvement action?
options: Stop issuing test certificates to clients
Ask clients not to read their certificates
Find why readings are missed and fix the process
Fill in the missing readings from memory

questions.stem: Why draw a flowchart (process map) of how a breakdown call is handled, from the phone call to the invoice?
options: To decorate the office notice board
To see each step and spot delays and waste
To replace the need for any job sheets
To show how many hours the crew works

questions.stem: A trial shows a battery-powered crimping tool saves time, but it costs more than the team's budget allows. What should the leader do?
options: Buy it anyway on the company account
Drop the idea without telling anyone
Take the trial data and costs to the manager
Ask each crew member to chip in some money

questions.stem: Why set a review date when an improvement is brought in?
options: So its results are checked and it is adjusted if needed
So the change stops on that exact day, whatever has happened by then
So the crew knows when to go back to the old way
So the improvement can be kept secret until then

questions.stem: Which improvement also reduces the company's impact on the environment?
options: Leaving van engines running at every site
Throwing old fluorescent tubes in the skip
Printing every drawing three times over
Planning routes and recycling scrap copper

questions.stem: After a change to how ladders are carried on the vans, fewer ladders are damaged. What should be done with this result?
options: Nothing, since ladders are cheap to replace
Record it, share it and make it the standard
Change the method again straight away, before anyone gets used to it
Keep it within the one crew that tried it

questions.stem: A trial of a new method has failed to give better results. How should the team treat this?
options: As useful learning, recorded for next time
As proof that nothing should ever change
As a reason to discipline whoever suggested it
As something to hide from the manager

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: In the PDCA improvement cycle, what word does the letter 'C' stand for?
What is a board called that has the outline of each tool drawn on it, so that a missing tool is seen at once?
What name is given to the idea that about 80% of problems come from about 20% of causes?
A fishbone diagram is also known by which other name?
In 5S, which first step means taking out of the work area everything that is not needed?
What word names the measured starting point taken before a change, so that results can be compared afterwards?
Cable wasted per house fell from 60 m to 48 m after cuts were planned from the drawings. What is the percentage reduction?
After a 5S clean-up, the time to find a set of parts in the van fell from 10 minutes to 4 minutes. What is the percentage saving?
What is an event called in which nobody was hurt but someone could have been, such as a ladder slipping with nobody on it?
After an improvement is proved, what is the written step-by-step method called that becomes the standard way of doing the task?
What type of diagram uses boxes and arrows to show each step of a process in order?
What is the name of a system in which workers put forward ideas for improvement, often through a box or an online form?
A J$90,000 tool saves J$15,000 a month. What is its payback period, in months?
What one word names the kind of waste in which workers stand idle, for example while they wait for an inspector or for materials?
What word names a planned check of records and work against the company's system, to find out whether procedures are being followed?

essays.stem: Explain what continuous improvement means. Then describe the four steps of the PDCA cycle, using the example of reducing failed inspections on new house wiring.
essays.modelAnswer: Continuous improvement means always looking for better ways to work, in small, planned steps, and keeping the changes that work. It never stops: after one improvement, the team looks for the next. The PDCA cycle is a simple way to do this. Plan: the team studies the problem using data. For example, the records show that 6 of the last 20 new houses failed their first inspection, mostly for missing bonding and missing labels. The team finds the causes and plans a change, such as a handover checklist that the lead signs before booking the inspection, with a target of fewer than 1 in 20 failures. Do: the checklist is trialled on the next few jobs. Check: the team compares the inspection results with the starting figure and asks the crews what worked. Act: if the results are better, the checklist is written into the procedure and all crews are trained; if not, the team changes the plan and goes round the cycle again.
markingPoints: Defines continuous improvement as ongoing, step-by-step improvement
Plan: uses data, finds causes and sets a target
Do: trials the change on a small scale
Check: compares results with the starting point
Act: standardises or adjusts and repeats

essays.stem: Describe how a lead electrician can involve the crew in continuous improvement, and explain why this matters.
essays.modelAnswer: The crew does the work every day, so they see the delays, waste and problems first. If they are involved, the ideas are more practical and they are more willing to use the changes. A lead electrician can make improvement part of normal work by asking at each weekly meeting, 'What slowed us down this week?' and 'What could we do better?'. Ideas can also come through a suggestion form or a simple board in the workshop. Every idea should be thanked and recorded, and the person told what happens to it. The lead can let the person who suggested an idea help plan and run a small trial and collect the results. Results should be shared with the whole crew, using simple charts. Good ideas should be recognised, for example by naming the person at a meeting or in a newsletter. The lead must also make it safe to report mistakes and near misses without blame, as these are often the best sources of improvement.
markingPoints: Explains that the crew knows the real problems and will own the changes
Collects ideas through meetings, forms or a board
Thanks, records and gives feedback on every idea
Involves the crew in trials and shares results
Recognises contributions and encourages blame-free reporting

essays.stem: Last quarter a contractor had 40 callbacks: loose terminations 18, wrong circuit labels 9, nuisance RCD trips 6, damaged accessories 4 and other causes 3. Put the causes in Pareto order, work out the share of the top two causes, and explain what the team should do next.
essays.modelAnswer: In Pareto order, from most to least: loose terminations 18, wrong circuit labels 9, nuisance RCD trips 6, damaged accessories 4, and other causes 3. The top two causes give 18 + 9 = 27 callbacks out of 40, which is 27 ÷ 40 = 67.5%, or about two thirds. This shows the team should work on loose terminations and labelling first, because fixing these few causes will remove most callbacks. Next, the team should look for the root causes of each, using the 5 whys or a fishbone diagram. For loose terminations, causes may be no torque screwdriver, rushed work at the end of a job or no final check. For labels, there may be no standard labelling method. The team would then plan changes, such as using torque screwdrivers set to the maker's figures, a 'tug test' on every conductor and a handover checklist with label checks. They would trial the changes, track callbacks each month on a chart, and compare them with this quarter's figures.
markingPoints: Puts the causes in the correct Pareto order
Calculates the top two as 27 of 40, or 67.5%
Says to tackle the top causes first, with the reason
Uses root cause tools to find why these happen
Plans, trials and monitors changes against the baseline

essays.stem: New installations keep failing inspection because the main earth bonding to the water pipe is missing. Show how the team could use the 5 whys to find the root cause, and say what improvement would follow.
essays.modelAnswer: The team starts with the problem and asks 'why?' until it reaches a cause it can fix. Why did the installation fail? Because the main bonding to the water pipe was missing. Why was it missing? Because the plumber fitted the pipe after the electricians had finished. Why was it not done later? Because nobody went back to fit it. Why did nobody go back? Because there was no step in our job plan to check for services added after first fix. Why was there no step? Because our job checklist was written for first fix only and has never been reviewed. The root cause is a gap in the job process, not one careless worker. The improvement would be to add a pre-inspection check of all bonding to the checklist, to agree with the builder that we are told when pipes are fitted, and to brief all crews. The team would then watch the inspection results for the next jobs to see whether the failures stop.
markingPoints: Starts from the clear problem statement
Asks a logical chain of 'why' questions
Reaches a process root cause rather than blaming a person
Proposes suitable improvements that fix the root cause
Plans to monitor the results

essays.stem: Describe four kinds of waste that can be found in an electrical contracting business. For each, give an example and an improvement.
essays.modelAnswer: Motion is unnecessary movement. For example, an electrician walks back to the van many times for parts. The improvement is a job kit list and a parts bag packed before going on site. Waiting is time when people cannot work, such as a crew standing idle because the inspector is late or materials have not arrived. The improvement is to book inspections early, confirm deliveries the day before and plan back-up tasks. Defects are mistakes that must be fixed, such as loose terminations that cause callbacks. The improvement is a standard method with torque screwdrivers and a final check before handover. Transport is unnecessary moving of people or materials, such as crews driving across the parish between jobs in no order. The improvement is grouping jobs by area. Other wastes include too much stock held in the stores and unused skills, when workers' ideas are not asked for. Cutting waste saves time and money and often improves quality and safety.
markingPoints: Names four correct types of waste
Gives a suitable electrical example for each
Gives a practical improvement for each
Explains the benefit of cutting waste
Examples are realistic for an electrical contractor

essays.stem: Explain how you would use the 5S method to organise a crew's van or the workshop stores, and how you would make sure the improvement lasts.
essays.modelAnswer: Sort: take everything out and keep only what is needed for the crew's normal work. Broken tools are repaired or thrown out, and items rarely used go back to the main store. Set in order: give everything a marked place, with the most-used items easiest to reach. Use labelled bins for fittings, a shadow board or foam tray for hand tools, and a secure, padded place for test instruments. Heavy drums go low down. Shine: clean the van or store, and at the same time check tools and leads for damage. Standardise: write a simple layout and a stock list with minimum levels, take a photo of the correct layout and fix it inside the door, so anyone can see what goes where. Sustain: set a short weekly check by the crew and a monthly check by the lead, using a scoring sheet. Results are shared and good scores recognised. Measuring the time to find items before and after shows the benefit and keeps the crew interested.
markingPoints: Sort: removes unneeded items
Set in order: a marked place for everything, by frequency of use
Shine: cleans and inspects
Standardise: layout, stock list and photos
Sustain: regular checks, scoring and measuring the benefit

essays.stem: A new procedure for recording test results is to be used by all crews. Explain how you would introduce it and deal with workers who resist the change.
essays.modelAnswer: I would start by explaining why the change is needed, using facts, such as an audit that found missing readings on 1 in 10 certificates and the risk this brings for safety and the company's name. I would show the new procedure and form at a crew meeting, demonstrate how to fill it in on a real example and let each person practise. I would make sure the written procedure is updated, old forms are removed from the vans and everyone has the new version. Some workers may resist because the old way is familiar or because they fear more paperwork. I would listen to their concerns and take them seriously; they may spot real problems, and the form can be improved. I would ask an experienced, respected electrician to help trial it. I would check the first certificates each person completes, give helpful feedback and share the results, such as fewer errors. If someone still refuses after support, I would explain that the procedure is required and report it to the manager.
markingPoints: Explains the reason for the change with facts
Briefs, demonstrates and lets people practise
Updates the procedure and removes old versions
Listens to concerns and involves respected staff
Checks early use, gives feedback and escalates if needed

essays.stem: Explain how you would monitor an improvement after it has been introduced, using the example of a new handover checklist, and what you would do if it was not working.
essays.modelAnswer: Before the checklist starts, I would record a baseline, such as the number of callbacks and first-time inspection failures each month for the last six months. I would set a clear target, for example halving callbacks within three months, and a review date. After the start, I would check that the checklist is really being used by looking at completed checklists for each job. Each month I would count callbacks and failures and plot them on a run chart against the baseline and target. I would also ask the crews and some clients what they think. At the review date I would compare the results with the target. If the checklist is working, it becomes part of the standard procedure. If it is not working, I would find out why: it may not be used properly, it may miss the real causes, or it may be too long. I would adjust it, retrain if needed, and continue to monitor, going round the PDCA cycle again.
markingPoints: Records a baseline and sets a target and review date
Checks that the change is actually being used
Measures results regularly and charts them
Collects feedback from crews and clients
Standardises if it works, or finds why not and adjusts

essays.stem: Explain why a contractor should record and share the lessons learned from improvement projects and jobs, and describe how this can be done.
essays.modelAnswer: If lessons are not recorded, the same mistakes are made again, good ideas stay with one crew, and knowledge is lost when experienced workers leave. Recording and sharing lessons helps every crew work better and saves time and money. After each improvement project, and after any large job or incident, the team can hold a short review: what was planned, what happened, what went well, what went badly and what to do differently. The lead writes this on a simple lessons-learned form. The forms are kept in a shared, organised file or database, with headings so they are easy to search, for example by type of job or problem. Lessons that change the way work is done are written into the procedures and training. Key points are shared at crew meetings and toolbox talks. Experienced workers can be asked to record what they know about a client's installation in notes and marked-up drawings before they retire. The file should be reviewed regularly so it stays useful.
markingPoints: Explains why: avoid repeating mistakes, spread good ideas, keep knowledge
Describes a short review after projects or jobs
Uses a standard form and a shared, searchable store
Builds lessons into procedures, training and meetings
Captures experienced workers' knowledge and keeps the file up to date

essays.stem: A crew member suggests that, to save time, insulation tests should only be done on some circuits in each house. Explain how you would judge this idea and any improvement idea, and what you would decide.
essays.modelAnswer: I would judge every improvement idea against a few questions. Is it safe? Does it keep the work legal and to the specification? What is the benefit, in time, money or quality? What does it cost in money, effort and training? What are the risks, and can they be controlled? Can it be trialled and measured? For this idea, the time saving is real but small, while the risk is serious. Insulation testing finds damaged cables, nails through cables and wiring faults that cannot be seen. A circuit that is not tested could have a fault that causes a fire or a shock, and the certificate would not be true. Leaving out tests would also break the specification and the testing rules. So I would thank the crew member, explain clearly why the idea cannot be used, and turn it into a better question: how can we make testing quicker while still testing every circuit? For example, the team could use a test sequence sheet, better lead sets or pre-printed certificates, and trial those instead.
markingPoints: Gives sound criteria: safety, compliance, benefit, cost and risk
Explains the purpose of insulation testing every circuit
Identifies the safety and legal risks of the idea
Decides to reject it and explains this respectfully
Redirects to a safe way of saving time

practical1.title: Carry out a 5S improvement on an electrical stores area and measure the result
practical1.brief: The assessor chooses an electrical stores shelf, tool cupboard or training van bay at the Centre that needs organising, and gives a list of 10 items a crew often needs. Nothing in the area is connected to a supply. First, measure the baseline: two members each time how long it takes to collect the 10 items, and the group photographs the area 'before'. Then apply 5S, sharing the work so every member leads at least one step: Sort (red-tag and remove items not needed, with the instructor's approval for anything to be thrown away); Set in order (give everything a labelled place, most-used items easiest to reach, heavy items low, with a shadow board or outlines for hand tools); Shine (clean the area and inspect tools and leads, tagging any damaged ones); Standardise (make a layout photo sheet, labels and a stock list with minimum levels); and Sustain (write a weekly 5S check sheet with a simple score). Finally, the same two members time the 10-item collection again, and the group works out the time saved as a percentage and writes a one-page improvement report. Photograph each stage below.
materials: A stores shelf, tool cupboard or van bay chosen by the assessor
List of 10 commonly needed items (supplied by the assessor)
Red tags, labels, a label maker or marker pens, and storage bins
Board and marker for a shadow board, or outline tape
Stopwatch or phone timer; stock list, check sheet and report forms
photos: The area before, with the baseline times recorded
The labelled layout and shadow board after Set in order
The cleaned area and any damaged items tagged
The layout photo sheet, stock list and weekly check sheet
The area after, with the new times and the improvement report
checklist: Took part in measuring the baseline accurately
Led at least one 5S step and explained it
Inspected tools and leads and tagged damaged items
Helped write the standard and the sustain check sheet
Worked safely and kept others informed
safety: No electrical work: nothing in the area is energised, and only the instructor may energise anything at the Centre
Use safe manual handling: two people for cable drums and heavy boxes, and keep heavy items low
Wear gloves when handling sharp off-cuts, trunking and metal parts
Throw nothing away without the instructor's approval; put scrap copper and lamps in the correct bins

practical2.title: Analyse callback data and present a PDCA improvement plan to management (role play)
practical2.brief: The assessor gives your group a contractor's data for the last two quarters: callbacks and inspection failures by cause, job sheets with times, and a few client comments. As a group, analyse the data and plan an improvement. Share the roles: one member makes a check sheet and draws a Pareto chart of the causes; one draws a fishbone diagram for the biggest cause and writes a 5 whys chain to find its root cause; one writes a PDCA plan with a SMART target, the change to be trialled, who does what, the measures, the baseline and a review date; one drafts the new or changed procedure or checklist; and one prepares a one-page poster that tells the crews about the change and why it matters. Then role-play a meeting: two members present the plan to the 'operations manager' (the assessor or a member using the role card), who questions the cost, the safety and the benefits; the others answer and one takes notes. Swap so every member speaks at least once. Photograph each stage below.
materials: Callback, inspection and job sheet data, and client comments (supplied by the assessor)
Manager's role card (supplied by the assessor)
Graph paper, poster paper, rulers and coloured markers
Blank check sheet, fishbone, 5 whys, PDCA plan and procedure forms
photos: The check sheet and Pareto chart
The fishbone diagram and the 5 whys chain
The PDCA plan with target, measures and review date
The presentation to the manager, at each change of speaker
checklist: Counted and ranked the causes correctly
Used the fishbone and 5 whys to reach a real root cause
Set a SMART target with a baseline and review date
Planned a change that is safe, practical and measurable
Drafted clear, simple procedure steps or poster wording
Explained the plan and answered the manager's questions
safety: This is a desk and role-play task: no electrical work is done
No proposed change may remove safe isolation, testing or supervision
Use only the made-up data supplied; do not use real client or staff names
Respect each other's ideas in the meeting; no personal remarks
